posts.title: The autumn kozo pressing, sheet by sheet
posts.excerpt: The first cool mornings are back, and so is the vat. A morning with Sayo as the autumn kozo goes from bark to board.
posts.content:
The vat house smells different in October. The water is colder, the bark has been soaking for a week, and Sayo is in before seven, sleeves rolled, testing the fibre between her fingers like dough.

Why autumn paper is better

Cold water keeps the fibres from swelling too fast and holds the formation aid thick and slippery, so each sheet knits evenly. Summer paper is fine; autumn paper is a little stronger, a little quieter under the pen.

A good sheet is quiet. You only notice it when you write.

Sayo, at the vat

This pressing is the kozo writing sheet and the heavier deckle-edge letter paper. Both reach the shop at the end of the month, once they have dried on the boards and rested a week in the dark.

If you would like to lift a sheet yourself, the October vat workshops still have a few seats.

posts.title: Grinding ink slowly, and why it is worth ten minutes
posts.excerpt: Tomoe on the stone, the stick and the little pool of water that turns into the darkest ink you will ever write with.
posts.content:
Most people meet sumi in a bottle. That is fine for a busy day, but grinding your own is a different thing: ten minutes of slow circles that settle the hand before the first stroke.

Stone, stick, water

  • A few drops of water in the well of the stone
  • The stick held upright, moved in small, even circles
  • Push the ink into the well, add water, repeat until it coats the stone

The ink is ready when a line on scrap paper dries without a grey halo. Thicker for lettering, thinner for washes. Rinse the stone straight after; dried ink is hard to lift.

The ink is never in a hurry, so neither am I.

Tomoe, grinding before a workshop

posts.title: A letter a month: our small autumn practice
posts.excerpt: One letter, by hand, on the first Sunday of every month. How the three of us keep it up, and how to start your own.
posts.content:
It started as a dare between the three of us: one handwritten letter a month, to anyone, for a year. That was four years ago, and none of us has missed a month since.

How to begin

  • Pick the day now: ours is the first Sunday
  • Keep a short list of people who would be glad of a letter
  • Write one side of one sheet, no more
  • Post it the same day, before you reread it

The trick is the size. One side of an A5 sheet is short enough to finish over a cup of tea and long enough to say something real.

posts.title: Sewing a four-hole binding at the kitchen table
posts.excerpt: Ren’s notes on the simplest binding there is: four holes, one needle, a length of waxed linen and an hour on a quiet evening.
posts.content:
The four-hole stab binding is the first thing Ren teaches and still the one he sews most. It needs no glue and no press, only a needle, an awl and a little patience.

What you need

  • Forty to sixty folded sheets and two cover sheets
  • An awl, a ruler and two clips
  • A blunt needle and waxed linen thread, four times the height of the book

Clamp the pages, pierce four holes a finger’s width from the spine, and sew around the spine and the head and tail in a figure that comes back to where it started. The knot hides inside the second hole.

Four holes, one needle, and the patience to go back when it’s crooked.

Ren, at the long table

posts.title: Three ways to wrap a gift in cloth and paper
posts.excerpt: A square of cotton, an offcut of kozo and a length of string: three simple wraps we use at the counter every day.
posts.content:
We wrap every order by hand, and over the years three wraps have stayed. None needs tape, and all of them can be undone and used again.

The cloth knot, the paper fold, the string bundle

The cloth knot is the furoshiki you know: the gift in the middle, two corners tied, then the other two. The paper fold is a kozo offcut folded over twice and tucked into itself. The string bundle is for letters and flat things: cross the string once and tie it with a bow you can pull open.

The furoshiki gift set comes in the first; every other order leaves in the second.

posts.title: New shelves, longer hours, and a seat by the window
posts.excerpt: We have moved downstairs. The new room has longer shelves, a window seat for trying pens and twelve places at the long table.
posts.content:
After seventeen years above the vat house, the atelier has moved to the ground floor next door. The old room was lovely and impossible to reach with a pram, a wheelchair or a box of paper.

What is new

  • Open Wednesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 18:00
  • A window seat with paper and pens to try
  • Twelve seats at the workshop table, step-free

The old room upstairs stays as Sayo’s drying room, so the shop smells of fresh paper on pressing days.

posts.title: Carving your first seal: notes from the summer workshop
posts.excerpt: Eleven people, eleven blanks of cherry wood and one very sharp knife each. What we learned at the July seal workshop.
posts.content:
The seal workshop always starts quiet. Everyone draws their mark in pencil, then has to draw it again in reverse, and the room goes still while people turn their paper over to check.

Three things Tomoe always says

  • Carve away from the line, never towards it
  • Keep the knife still and turn the wood
  • Stop when you think you need one more cut

By the end, eleven new seals were printed in persimmon ink on the back of a letter sheet. The next seal workshop is on the last Saturday in November.

products.name: Kozo Writing Sheets
products.short: Twenty thin, strong sheets of kozo paper with a soft deckle edge, for letters, brush and fountain pen. A5.
products.description:
Our everyday writing paper, made at the Kurata vat house from mulberry bark that is cooked, picked clean by hand and beaten on a stone. The long fibres stay visible in the sheet, so every page is slightly different, and the surface is sized just enough to take fountain-pen ink without feathering.

Write on the smoother side, fold along the grain, and keep the sheets flat in their paper sleeve.

products.name: Deckle-Edge Letter Paper
products.short: Ten heavier sheets of kozo and cotton with four torn edges, for letters you mean to keep. A4.
products.description:
A heavier sheet for the letters that matter: invitations, thank-yous, a page you hope someone keeps in a drawer for years. Each sheet is formed one at a time and keeps all four deckle edges.

Brush, dip pen and fountain pen all sit well on it. Fold once, gently, with a bone folder.

products.name: Indigo Thread-Bound Notebook
products.short: Ninety-six blank pages of smooth kozo paper, sewn by hand with linen thread into an indigo-dyed cover. B6.
products.description:
Ren sews these one at a time at the long table by the window: a four-hole stab binding in waxed linen thread, through a cover dyed in indigo by a small workshop up the valley. The pages are blank, smooth and opaque enough for ink on both sides.

It opens flat once it has been used for a week or two. Like all indigo, the cover softens and lightens a little with handling.

products.name: Plain Field Journal
products.short: A lay-flat journal of cream paper that takes fountain-pen ink without feathering. A5, 160 pages.
products.description: The notebook we use ourselves for orders, sketches and lists. Cream paper, sewn in signatures so it lies flat on the first day, with a plain cloth spine and no lines to tell you where to write.

products.name: Brush Pen Trio
products.short: Three refillable brush pens: indigo, persimmon and a pale water brush for soft washes.
products.description: Fine synthetic tips that spring back to a point, in plain bamboo-coloured barrels. The indigo and persimmon pens hold enough ink for weeks of letters; the third holds clean water for softening a line into a wash.

products.name: Inkstone & Ink Stick
products.short: A small slate inkstone on a hinoki tray, with a pine-soot ink stick for grinding your own sumi.
products.description:
Grinding ink takes ten quiet minutes and changes how you write: the ink is as dark as you choose, and the first line after it feels earned. This set has everything you need except the water.

Rinse the stone after use and let it dry face up.

products.name: Indigo Sumi Ink, 60 ml
products.short: Ready-ground ink with a blue undertone that dries to a deep, quiet indigo. For brush and dip pen.
products.description: For the days without ten minutes to grind. Our liquid sumi is mixed with a little indigo, so a heavy stroke dries nearly black and a light one shows its blue. Not for fountain pens.

products.name: Kozo Letter Set
products.short: Eight letter sheets and six envelopes of soft white kozo, tied with cotton string.
products.description: Enough for a month of letters if you write one a week and spoil two. The sheets fold into the envelopes in thirds; the envelopes are glued by hand and close with a little water or a seal.

products.name: Blank Seal Stamp Set
products.short: Five uncarved cherry-wood blanks, round and square, for carving your own seal at home or in a workshop.
products.description: Soft enough for a beginner's knife, hard enough to keep a fine line. Draw your mark in reverse with a pencil, carve slowly, and test on scrap paper. Tomoe's seal workshop starts with exactly these.

products.name: Persimmon Seal Ink Pad
products.short: A brass-rimmed pad of soft persimmon-red paste for seals and stamps. Autumn price while it lasts.
products.description: A slightly warmer red than the usual cinnabar, the colour of a ripe persimmon. Press the seal gently twice, stamp on a soft surface, and close the lid between uses so the paste stays supple.

products.name: Furoshiki Gift Set
products.short: A letter set, a brush pen and a small notebook, wrapped in a persimmon cotton furoshiki with an indigo knot.
products.description: Our most given gift. Everything for a first letter, wrapped in a cotton cloth that becomes the next wrapping, a scarf or a cover for a bowl. We add a handwritten card if you tell us the name.
